ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Allocation under SGRY to Gujarat 
*461. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENTbe pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government have any scheme to launch Sampoma 
Grameen RozgarYojna; 
(b) if so, the salient features thereof; and 
(c) the funds allocated/proposed to be allocated to the State of Gujarat 
under the scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M. K. PAITL): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Government launched the Sampooma Grameen Rozgar Yojna 
(SGRY) 
on 25th September, 2001 and the Scheme is in operation throughout the 
country. 
(b) The Sampooma Grameen Rozgar  Yojna (SGRY) was launched to 
provide additional wage employment and food security to the rural poor 
through 
creation of need-based infrastructure in  the rural areas. The Scheme is being 
implemented through the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs). The funds and 
1 

RAJYA SABHA            [23 April, 2003] 
foodgrains are distributed among the District Panchayats, Intermediate Level 
Panchayats and Gram Panchayats in the ratio of 20:30:50. The wages are paid 
to the workers partly in foodgrains and partly in cash. However, a minimum 
25% of the wages is required to be paid in cash. 
(c) During the current year (2003-2004), an amount of Rs. 89.66 crores 
alongwith 96725 MTs of foodgrains has been allocated under the Sampooma 
Grameen Rozgar Yojana (Stream-I and Stream-II) to the State Government of 
Gujarat

[23 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
THEMINISTEROF STATEINTHEMMSTRYOFPERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) 
and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The Approach Paperto the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002—
2007) focuses on governance as a critical factor for promotion of economic 
development The formulation of viable schemes for bringing about 
development especially in the social sector and an appropriate delivery 
system to implement such schemes have been identified for the above 
purpose and good governance has been identified as intrinsic to both. 
Transparency in governmental functioning, greater accountability across all 
the sectors of government, use of information technology so as to reduce 
discretion and delay, security of tenure, tackling corruption and strengthening 
the rule of law, promotion of gender equality have been, inter-alia, the 
governance reforms suggested.

constituted on 19 February, 2003 to formulate specific changes in the systems 
and procedures, in consultation with Ministries/Departments concerned, and 
to devise strategies for changing attitudes. The Group is required to prepare 
an Action Plan for implementation of its recommendations within a time-

constituted on 20 February, 2003. 
3. The first meeting of the Core Group on Administrative Reforms 
(CGAR) was held on 3 March, 2003, in which the following eight subjects 
were identified for preparing Concept Papers along with Action Plans: 
(i) How to make the administration efficient and transparent? 
(ii) How to make the administration responsive and citizen-friendly? 
(iii) How to make the administration accountable? 
(iv) Simplification of rules, regulations and procedures and creating 
public awareness about them; 
(v) Delegation of authority from 'nodal' Ministries, to 'functional' 
Ministries, within the Ministries and from the Ministries to their 
field offices;

Package for SEBs 
 *476.    SHRI GAYA SINGH :††                   
SHRI V.V.RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that Govern ment have allocated Rs. 40,000 
crore as package to reform the State Electricity Boards; and 
(b) if so, the details of the package and steps proposed to be taken to 
reduce the losses of the Boards? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM 
GEETE): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The Government has approved the Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) during the 10th Plan period 
for upgradation of distribution system covering densely electrified zones 
focusing on urban and industrial areas. The proposed outlay is Rs. 40.000 
crores, comprising of Rs. 20,000 crores towards investment component and 
another Rs. 20,000 crores towards the incentive component. The funding 
through budgetary support on a yearly basis would be based on need, 
utilization and availability of funds. The Programme aims at reducing the 
cash losses to improve financial viability of the State Electricity Boards 
(SEBs)/ Utilities. The programme has tw o components, namely investment 
component and incentive component to encourage/motivate utilities to reduce 
cash losses. Under the investment scheme, APDRP will finance specific 
projects 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Gaya 
Singh. 
30 

   [23 April, 2003]                RAJYASABHA 
relating to upgradation and strengthening of subtransmission & distribution 
network including, inter alia, energy accounting & metering. The incentive 
scheme aims at actual cash loss reduction by SEBs/Utilities. Under this 
scheme, grant amounting to fifty per cent of the actual cash loss reduction 
effected by SEB/Utility would be provided. 
Under the Memorandum of Agreement signed between the SEBs and 
the Ministry of Power, the SEBs have agreed for taking steps to reduce the 
losses and to reduce outages and interruptions and thus reduce Aggregate 
Technical & Commercial losses. These steps, inter-alia, include metering of 
11 KV feeders and all consumers; un dertake energy audit at all levels; 
upgrading and stengthening of distribution system; introduction of 
Information Technology for automation, billing & collection of revenue, etc.

Important measure taken to prevent, out-break of fire are listed 
below.— 
In underground mines: 
(i) Extraction of coal by forming panels of proper size which can be 
extracted within the incubation period. 
(ii) Constructing preparatory stoppings to enable quick isolation of 
the panel in case of out-break of fire. 
(iii) Monitoring environmental conditions in extraction areas, sealed 
off areas, old workings, return airways for early detection of 
fires. 
(iv) Blanketing of surface areas over extracted areas. 
(v) Inspection of workings, isolation/fire-stoppings, including old 
workings on idle days. 
(vi) Environmental tele-monitoring systems are being installed in a 
phased manner in some fiery and highly gassy underground 
mines. Already thirteen such sy stems are in operation and two 
more such systems are under procurement. 
In opencast mines: 
(i) Blanketing of exposed benches in coal seams prone to 
spontaneous heating and in coal stocks. 
(ii) Provision for waler-spraying. 
(iii) Regular inspection of coal dumps, OB dumps, stocks etc.

Judicious exploitation of mineral resources 
3492. SHRI R. P. GOE NKA : Will the Minister of MINES be pleased 
to State: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to a recent report 
entitled "undermining Inc ia" brought out by Kalpvariksh, a Non-
Governmental Organisation highligthing that indiscriminate mining of 
bauxite, iron ore, lime stone etc. in certains parts of the country is destroying 
some of the most ecologically sensitive areas, including catchment mat 
provide water to millions of people, and is a threat to long term water 
security; 
(b) if so, the Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) details of fresh strategies drawn up for a more judicious exploitation 
of the mineral resources of the country ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES (SHRI 
RAMESHBAIS): (a) to (c) The Ministry of Mines, Government of India is 
aware of recent Newspaper reports on the concerns expressed in a study done 
by Kalpavariksh, a non-Governmenta l Organisation, in their report 
"Undermining India". 
The National Mineral Policy, 1993 (NMP), inter alia recognizes that 
the policies governing the mining and mineral sector should be harmonized 
with the policies governing industrial and socio-economic developments in 
the country. Some mineral rich areas are ecologically fragile and some are 
biologically rich. 
117 

RAJYA SABHA                     [23 April, 2003] 
NMP states that it is necessary to take comprehensive view to facilitate the 
choice or order of land use keeping in view the needs of development as well 
as needs of protecting the forests, environment and ecology. Both aspects 
have to be properly coordinated to  facilitate and ensure a sustainable 
development of mineral resources in harmony with environment. 
As envisaged in the NMP, in order to ensure scientific and systematic 
mining with due regard to environment, under mining statutes, no mining 
lease can be granted without an approved mining plan. Stringent penalties 
have been provided for violations of Mineral Conservation and Development 
Rules, 1988. Mining activities are also subject to other laws of the land 
including the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Forest (Conservation) 
Act, 1980 and rules made thereunder. Mi ning industry is also required to 
follow the air pollution and water pollution norms. For major mining projects 
of bauxite, iron ore, limestone etc., public hearing and environmental impact 
assessment studies are required before mining leases are granted. In addition, 
mining in ecologically fragile regions is restricted under specific Regulations 
and Notifications like the Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, Aravalli 
Notification, etc. 
The independent studies and reports on effect of mining on environment 
brought out from time to time help the Government in taking policy decisions 
and streamlining the monitoring mechanism for sustainable development of 
mineral resources in harmony with environment, which is an ongoing 
process.

3495. PROF. R. B. S. VARMA: Will the Minister of PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS be pleased to state:

can review its final allocation orders in case of the division of any State in the

Court;  
(c) if not, the reasons therefor;

allocation orders, on receipt of the r ecommendations of the State Advisory

regards SERCs, States have been given flexibility in regard to setting up of 
Regulatory Commissions as also in terms of conferring certain functions on 
them. Sub-section (1) of section 22 of the Act stipulates mandatory functions 
of SERCs while Sub-section (2) of sec tion 22 provides for optional functions 
which may be conferred upon the

Commissions on some other aspects of regulation as well.

Power to neighbouring states by DPP 
3504. SHRISURESH PACHOURI: W ill the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to State: 
(a) whether Government of Maharashtra is working on revival of 
Dabhol Power Project; 
(b) if so,whether the Central Government has taken any initiative in this 
regard; 
(c)once operationalised, whether there is any proposal to sell surplus 
power to neighbouring State like Madhya Pradesh; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) Government of Maharashtra 
(GOM) has taken a decision to allow th e Maharashtra State Electricity Board 
(MSEB) to draw power from Phase-I (740 MW) of Dabhol Power Project at 
an optimum level of 83% at a tariff of about Rs. 2.80/KWH of an interim 
basis subject to approval of the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory 
Commission (MERC) and High Court of Maharashtra which has appointed a 
receiver for the project, and without prejudice to MSEB/GOM's rights and 
contentions in the pending arbitration/ judicial and MERC proceedings. 
(b) The power Purchase Agreement (PPA) in regard to the Dabhol 
Power Project was entered into between MSEB and Dabhol Power Company 
(DPC). Thus, the responsibility to restart Phase-I and complete Phase-II of 
the Dabhol project lies with the main stakeholders viz. MSEB and DPC as 
well as the Government of Maharashtra. The Indian Financial Institutions 
(IFIs) led by the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI), having 
substantial stakes in the Dabhol Power Project, have been trying to 
restructure and revive the Dabhol plant. Government of India has agreed to 
facilitate any amicable solution to the various issues in order to revive/ 
restructure the project. Any scheme finalized for revival of the Dabhol 
project would come as a comprehensive package and would have to resolve 
complex, legal, financial and technical issues. While this may take time, as a 
first step, it has been agreed that an interim revival package for restarting 
Phase-I be worked out by the concerned agencies. It has been decided that 
the National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) would act as the 
 129 
 

RAJYA SABHA            [23 April, 2003] 
Operation & Maintenance Contractor for running Phase-I. At the instance of 
the Government of India (Ministry of Power), a team involving 
representatives from NTPC, M/s GE I ndia, M/s Bechtel, IDBI, MSEB and 
Central Electricity Authority carried out a preliminary inspection of the 
Dabhol power plant from Oct. 28-30, 2002 to ascertain its condition and to 
work out an action plan for restart of phase-1. 
(c) Under the proposed scheme mentioned above, the power generated 
from Phase-I would be absorbed by MSEB. No decision has been taken and 
conveyed to the Government of India with regard to off-take of power from 
phase-II after it is completed. 
(d) The question of selling of surplus power (if any), from the Dabhol 
power project to neighbouring States like Madhya Pradesh, would be decided 
by the Government of Maharashtra and would depend upon the overall 
restructuring of the Dabhol Plant and related issues such as quantum of off-
take of power by Maharashtra and the final power tariff etc. after completion 
of phase-II.

(b) The Government has approved the Accelearated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) for upgradation of 
distribution system covering densely electrified zones focusing on urban and 
industrial areas. The proposed outlay for the programme is Rs. 40,000 crores, 
comprising of Rs. 20,000 crores towards investment component and another 
Rs. 20,000 crores towards the incentive component in the 10th Five Year 
Plan. The actual funding through budget ary support on a yearly basis would 
be based on need, utilization and availability of funds. The Programme aims 
at reducing the cash losses to improve financial viability of the State 
Electricity Boards (SEBs)AJtilities. The programme has two components, 
namely investment component and incentive component to 
encourage/motivate utilities to reduce cash losses. Under the investment 
scheme, APDRP will finance specific projects relating to upgradation and 
strengthening of sub-transmission & distribution network including energy 
accounting & metering in the distributi on circles in a phased manner. The 
incentive scheme aims at actual cash loss reduction by SEBs/Utilities. Under 
this scheme, grant amounting to fifty per cent of the actual cash loss 
reduction effected by SEBs Utilities would be provided. 
(c) All the State Electricity Boards/Utilities in the States are eligible for 
assistance under the Programme. 
(d) The activities taken up under APDRP would result in the following 
measurable outcomes: 
 
> Reduction of AT&C losses from the existing around 50% to 
around 15% in five years to begin with in the urban areas and 
high density/ consumption areas; 
> Significant improvement in revenue realization by reduction 
commercial losses leading to additional realization of an 
additional Rs. 20,000 crores, approximately over a period of 4 
to 5 years; 
> Reduction of technical losses would result in additional energy 
of nearly 6,000—7,000 MW to the system, avoiding the need of 
9,000 to 11,000 MW of fresh capacity additional besides 
avoiding investments to the tune of Rs. 40,000 to Rs. 60,000 
crores; 
> Quality of supply and reliable,  interruption-free power will 
encourage usage of energy e fficient equipments/appliances, 
which will further lead to improvement in availability of energy.

3522. SHRIJANARDHANA POOJAR Y: Will the Minister of

Electricity Boards are in a precariou s position with total transmission and 
distribution (T&D) losses accounting for Rs. 30,000 crores annually; 
(b) if so, the measures initiated by Government to mitigate the situation; 
 
(c) whether it is a fact that the Centre proposes to launch an incentive 
scheme to help States to minimize the T&D losses; and 
(d) if so, the details of the scheme and the States which have so far 
qualified for the incentive?

(SffiUMATI JAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) To improve the financial viability of the State Electricity Boards 
(SEBs)/Utilities the Central Government  have launched the Accelerated 
Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP). The Programme has two 
components, namely, investment component and incentive component. Under 
investment component, the Central Government provides assistance to the 
tune 
of 50% ( by way of loan and matching grant) of the project cost for the 
upgradation and modernization of distribution system in high density load 
centres 
like towns and industrial centres in non special cat egory states and 100% 
assistance (by way of 90% grant and 10%  loan) in case of special category 
states.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES

international market it is desirable to utilize all resources optimally and

of

from 
Gherzi Textile Organisation. The main findings of the study include:— 
• India's very low productivity (yield per hectare) results' in higher 
cost of raw cotton. 
• Power cost plays an important role more due to the factor cost, in 
the manufacturing cost of cotton textiles. 
• Inadequate investment across the value chain restricting growth of 
technologically upgraded capacity and the quality of out-put of the 
cotton textile industry, possible due to relative high cost of capital. 
• If the current scenario continues, i ndustry's present market share in 
the global market may shrink and ma y lead to adversely impact the 
domestic market. 
It is for the individual units to explore the possibilities for decreasing 
the cost of production by adopting various measures in order to remain 
competitive in the international market.

SHRI MATI N. P. DURGA  (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, it 
gives me immense pleasure to speak on this Bill which has been brought 
before us to amend sections 2 and 3 of the Prevention of Insults to National 
Honour Act, 1971.1 wholeheartedly welcome the move of the Government. 
Sir, flying the National Flag is governed by the Emblem and Names 
(Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 195 0, and the Prevention of Insults to 
National Honour Act, 1971. And, the Flag code brings together all such laws, 
conventions, practices and instructi ons for guidance and benefit of all 
concerned. As the House is aware, th e National Flag was adopted by the 
constituent Assembly on 22nd Jury, 1947, and all our National Symbols 
National Flag, State Emblem, National Anthem, National Song, National 
Calendar, National Animal, National Bird and National Flower derived their 
sanctity from our constitution. 
We have become independent and have got the pride of having our 
own 
269 

RAJYASABHA [23 April, 2003] 
National Mag after sacrifices made by millions of our people. We are honouring 
the National Flag. But alas! We have given little recognition to a great patriot, 
freedom fighter and architect of our Nati onal Flag. With your permission, I 
would just say a few lines on this. In our country, for the first time, we had 
unfurled our flag on 7th August, 1906, at Green Park in Calcutta. It had got the 
colours of red, yellow and green, with flowers and written on it 'Vande 
Mataram'. With some minor changes, almost similar kind of flag was unfurled in 
1907. In 1917, one more flag was prepared with 7 stars. But, in 1921, the 
Congress came under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi and met at 
Vijayawada in Andhra Pradesh. There, a young patriot, Shri Pingali Venkaiah, 
prepared our National Flag. He had done a lot of research, by that time, on the 
Indian Flag and had also written a book, called,' India's National Flag'. The 
National Flag was unfurled by the Home Rule Flag Union in Lucknow in 1916. 
But, when a meeting of the Congress took place in March, 1921, at 
Vijayawada, Shri Pingali Venkaiah showed the Flag prepared by him to 
Mahatma Gandhi. Bapu liked this Flag very much, and in 1931, the All India 
Congress Committee adopted this Flag. But, since 1921, this Flag was being 
unfurled, unofficially, in all the Congress and other meetings. The only 
difference between the Flag prepared by Shri Pingali Venkaiah and the present 
Flag is, now we have got the 'Dharma Chakra' in place of 'Ratna'. Sir, Mahatma 
Gandhi also wanted to adopt the Flag as it is, but the problem is that the Flag 
should look identifical from the front side and the backside. And if'Ratna' were 
retained, it would not have looked identica l. This is one of the main reasons for 
replacing 'Ratna' with Dharma Chakra'. Sir, Gandhiji had written appreciatingly 
about Shri Pingali Venkaiah in 'The Young India. ' But, what honour have we 
given to this great patriot? We have not done anything, literally. It pains us a lot 
because the great architect of this Flag  has not got the due recognition that he 
should have got. We have been, persistently, bringing this to the notice of the 
Government of India to honour him, but in vain. So, now, the time has come, 
and I thought that this is t he appropriate occasion to bring this to the notice of 
the Government of India. So, Madam, I request, through y ou, the Government 
of India to release a postal stamp and erect a statue of Shri Pingali Venkaiah in 
the premises of this great democratic in stitution, which, I am sure, would be a 
befitting tribute to this great man a nd freedom fighter who has given us the 
National Flag. 
The next point is: I welcome the inclusion of this explanation which 
makes it further clear as to what all constitutes disrespect to the National Flag. 
But, 
270 

[23 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
does merely providing a law guarantee any respect? I strongly believe that 
legislations or codes will not make much difference unless and until a feeling 
of nationalism and patriotism is inculcat ed and efforts are made to associate 
people themselves with these National Symbols. Now, the National Anthem is 
being made available at various websites and it can be downloaded on mobile 
phones for ringer tones. I strongly oppose this. I oppose this because you 
should not stop the National Anthem abruptly. It is a sheer disrespect to our 
National Anthem. And, if you are using this as a ringer tone, you would stop it 
abruptly to attend your call. So, I strongly urge the hon. Minister to issue 
directions to the people concerned to stop using not only our National 
Anthem. But also our National Song as ringer tones. 
I would like to raise one more issue, that is, about westernisation of our 
culture, and how our people, especially, during cricket and other matches in 
other countries, show disrespect to our National Flag. The people in the West 
use their National Flag as shirts, caps, shorts tattoos, or use as some other 
draper. Our people are copying this and they have started painting their faces 
and bodies with the National Flag, and have started tattooing the National 
Flag on their cheeks, or, are getting the Flags stitched as shirt or trousers. Not 
only other people, but even our cricketers are embossing the National Flag on 
their gloves and pads. Does it not am ount to showing disrespect to the Flag, 
according to this Act? So, I request t he hon. Minister to take steps and stop 
the occurrence of these incidents, especially, in foreign countries. 
Madam, with these words, I whole heartedly support the move of the 
Government and request the hon. Minister to assure this House that the 
Government of India would honour Shri Pingali fenkaiah in a befitting manner 
by releasing a Postal Stamp and erecti ng a statue in the premises of the 
Parliament, immediately. Thank you, Madam.

*SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Madam, Deputy Chairperson, I rise to 
support this Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Bill on behalf 
of AIADMK. It is said that this amending Bill has been brought because 
incidents of disrespect to national flag and other national symbols had come to 
the notice of the Government. This am endment provides for punishment even 
for showing disrespect to national symbols. The new Section 3-A provides that 
if a person commits such offence second time or time and again, he will be 
given a punishment of at least one-year. But I request the Minister to consider 
giving more punishment to those who commit this offence again and again. 
The Home Ministry should not think that its duty is over by providing 
punishment for those who show disrespect to national symbols. The 
Government should take st eps to inculcate patriotic feelings in the people, 
particularly the youth. The Government should create such an atmosphere so 
that people respect national symbols on  their own. These days we find people 
waving national flags only in the cricket stadiums. This shows that national 
feelings should be inculcated in the yo uth in the way they like. Functions like 
Independence Day and Republic Day are celebrated only in Government 
Offices and schools and colle ges. The general public are not able to be a part 
of such functions. It is the duty of t he Government to see that such functions 
are held in the nooks and corners of the country with the help of NGOs and 
other such organisations. Patriotic f eelings should come on its own. Such 
environment should exist. 
Finally I wish to make one point This House is unanimous in its view that 
all those who show disrespect to the national symbols should be punished. But 
we should realize that we can respect the national symbol only if we protect 
our nation. There is a sayi ng in Tamil. The translation goes thus: We ought to 
have a wall in order to make a drawing. 
But when action is taken against those who want to divide the country, 
there are people who support such separatists. I wish to ask, are they 
patriots? Will it be wTong to punish such people? I request this august House 
to ponder over this. 
Madam, the centre should support the State Governments when action is 
taken against anti-nationals, separatis ts, supporters of terrorists and those 
who have regular contacts with banned organisations. A nation cannot 
progress just by showing respect to national symbols. Stringent action should 
be taken against anti-national forces.
